title: Streets and plans: urban and transport planning, and the municipal office

blocks.html: Checked against the sources as they stood on 2026-10-16.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Urban and transport planning decides what the land in a town is used for and where its streets, footpaths, cycle tracks and public transport go, and fixes those decisions in plans, such as a city’s master plan. India’s National Urban Transport Policy of 2006 holds that transport planning “is intrinsically linked to land use planning” and that both must be developed together.

The owners of a question about a ward’s streets are an urban or transport planner and the municipal town-planning office.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
You met the Wards Committee in an earlier section, where the councillor chairs and you attend for health advice. Questions about the ward’s streets reach that committee, and they are not yours to answer. Urban and transport planners decide what land is for and where streets, paths and buses go, and they write those decisions into plans.

The policy speaks of a master plan — a city’s plan for how its land is used and where its roads and transport go as it grows. The policy says “an integrated master plan needs to internalize the features of sustainable transport systems”. That was the policy’s intention in 2006. It is not a fact about any city today.

The curriculum this book follows names “the master and mobility plans that fix them”. No document this book holds defines a mobility plan. It is a planner’s word, and the planner is who you ask what it means for your town.

Now ask who holds the plan. Book 5, Policy process, framing and advocacy craft, showed you the Constitution’s Twelfth Schedule, the list of matters that municipalities may be given work on. Item 1 reads “Urban planning including town planning.”

Article 243W, which Book 5 also showed you, says the Legislature of a State “may, by law, endow” the municipalities with powers and authority. That includes functions “in relation to the matters listed in the Twelfth Schedule”. So whether your municipality makes the town plan depends on your State’s law, and this book does not hold that law.

The policy puts the work in the same place. It says responsibility for planning and carrying out urban transport “rests with the State governments and the municipal bodies”.

In the Union government, the Allocation of Business Rules give the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA) two departments, inserted by an amendment dated 22 July 2026. Item 4 of the Department of Urban Development reads “Town and Country Planning”. This is the Union’s business in the field.

Here is the row for your list of owners.

Field Owner Where to look
Urban and transport planning an urban or transport planner; the municipal town-planning office your municipal corporation’s town-planning office (ask the corporation which office makes and keeps the town plan); a university department of planning or architecture (advice); at the Union level, MoHUA’s Department of Urban Development, for national policy

The first two places are kinds of place, given as advice.

blocks.label: Illustration 1
blocks.html:
Start with a cycle track that was built and not used, and see what the policy says about it.

Open the National Urban Transport Policy (https://mohua.gov.in/static/uploads/2025/10/0da700a8b86f2faee310bd49592ee99a.pdf). Search for “cycle tracks”. Read paragraph 28. The safety of cyclists and pedestrians is to be addressed by “encouraging the construction of segregated rights of way for bicycles and pedestrians” — paths kept separate from motor traffic.

Read on into paragraph 29. The failure comes first: “It has been the experience that many such cycle tracks and pedestrian paths do not get used as initially envisaged.” Then the policy gives an explanation, and reports it only as “a view”. The view is that these facilities “are designed badly and without fully recognizing the limitations and problems faced by cyclists or pedestrians”. Its remedy is to build them “after an open debate on the designs with experts and the community that is expected to use them”.

Now read paragraph 30. The Central Government “would give priority to the construction of cycle tracks and pedestrian paths in all cities”.

Last, ask what you would need to know to say whether one lane on one road will be used. Its width. Where it starts and ends. The crossings. The shade. What the main road carries. You do not know how to judge any of these. A planner does. That is the field’s kind of answer: a design, and where it sits in a plan.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
Paragraph 29 reports an experience and “a view” about why. It is not a study, and it gives no count of how many tracks went unused. The policy is the Union’s statement of 2006 of what it “would” do and support. It does not tell you what your city’s plan says now, and this book holds no later version.

Nothing here says that a cycle lane changes how active people are, or their weight. That evidence is taught in Book 24, Physical activity and sedentary behaviour science.

blocks.label: Illustration 2
blocks.html:
A made-up meeting: the Wards Committee. The councillor reads a letter from the corporation’s engineer.

“The corporation will build a cycle lane. It can go along the main road or along the lane behind the market. The committee should send its view by Friday.”

The councillor turns to you.

“You’re the health person. Which one will get our people cycling?”

Start with what you can answer now. You can say who in the ward is least active, if the health department has a ward survey that measured it. You can also say that, whatever is built, the ward can count who uses it before and after, and you can help design that count. Both are yours.

Now the signal. About to act fires first: the committee sends its view on Friday, and the corporation will build what it recommends. Behind it is No test. You cannot say what result would show “the main road” or “behind the market” wrong.

You say: “I can tell you who in the ward is least active, and I can help count who uses the lane once it is built. Which route gets people cycling is a design question. That is outside what I can assess, and here is who can: the town-planning office, and through it an urban or transport planner. I’ll write to them today, so we have a reply before Friday.”

The curriculum this book follows gives the question in these words. Write it in five parts.

Part Your question
Decision The Wards Committee’s view on where the corporation builds the cycle lane: the main road or the lane behind the market. The councillor and the committee are waiting; the corporation’s engineer wants the view by Friday.
Context The ward has a main road and a lane behind the market (map attached). What the health department knows about who is least active in the ward is attached, if a survey exists. The committee’s aim is more walking and cycling among those who do least.
Question “what would make this ward’s streets walkable and cyclable for the least active, and which plan or budget does that sit in?”
Form A recommendation between the two routes, or a third, with the reasons a committee can follow; how sure you are and on what; the name of the plan the lane would sit in, and the budget its money would come from. I cannot judge street design; tell me what would make you change your recommendation.
Deadline Thursday, so the committee can discuss it before Friday. If it comes later, the committee sends its view without it.

The question goes to the municipal town-planning office, with a request that an urban or transport planner answer it. The “which plan or budget” half is what makes the reply useful later, because it tells you where the decision can still be changed.

Add the row to your contact list now; a later section shows how to keep it.

Field Owner Name and institution How you know them Last question asked Asked on Checked on
Urban and transport planning an urban or transport planner; the municipal town-planning office (yours to fill) what would make this ward’s streets walkable and cyclable for the least active, and which plan or budget that sits in

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The move is wrong when the question is yours: who in the ward is least active, how to count use before and after, how the ward would know whether anything changed. Those stay with you.

It is also wrong to route the question “will this bring obesity down?” to a planner. A planner can tell you whether a lane is likely to be used, not what that does to weight. That half is evidence on activity, taught in Book 24, Physical activity and sedentary behaviour science, and you say so.

points.html: Do not tell a committee that a cycle lane will get people cycling, or that it will bring obesity down. The 2006 transport policy itself records that many cycle tracks and pedestrian paths “do not get used as initially envisaged”.

The error is to say the Constitution makes town planning the municipality’s job. The Twelfth Schedule lists “Urban planning including town planning”, and Article 243W lets the State Legislature, by law, give municipalities that work. Who draws your town’s plan depends on your State’s law; ask the corporation, or trace it.
Always ask the second half of the question: which plan or budget does it sit in.

The National Urban Transport Policy you can read is the Union’s statement of 2006, in the words “would” and “should”. It does not tell you what any city’s plan says today, and this book holds no later version.

The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs’ Department of Urban Development holds “Town and Country Planning” as Union business, item 4 of its entry. It is not the office that decides your ward’s streets.

blocks.label: Common misreading
blocks.html: Reading the 2006 policy’s priority for cycle tracks as evidence that cycle tracks raise activity. The policy states what the Union would support and records that many tracks went unused; it measures nothing about activity or weight.

blocks.prompt: From memory: who owns a question about making a ward’s streets walkable and cyclable? Give the curriculum’s question in its words. Then say what the 2006 transport policy says about cycle tracks that were built and not used, and what it proposes.
blocks.answer: An urban or transport planner, and the municipal town-planning office. “What would make this ward’s streets walkable and cyclable for the least active, and which plan or budget does that sit in?” The policy says many cycle tracks and pedestrian paths do not get used as initially envisaged. One view is that they were designed badly, without recognising the problems cyclists and pedestrians face. It proposes building them after an open debate on the designs with experts and the community that will use them.

blocks.prompt: A made-up request: at the Wards Committee, the head of a government school asks a question. Would a footpath and a safe crossing on the road outside the school get more children walking to school? The committee meets again in a month. Write the question you would ask, in the five parts, and say who gets it and what stays yours.
blocks.answer:
Part Your question
Decision Whether the committee asks the corporation for a footpath and a crossing outside the school; the councillor and committee decide at next month’s meeting; the head of the school is waiting.
Context The road outside the school (map attached); how children reach school now, if the school has counted it; the aim is more children walking.
Question “What would make the road outside this school walkable for its children, and which plan or budget does that sit in?”
Form What to build and where, how sure you are and on what, and the plan and budget it sits in; I cannot judge road design.
Deadline A week before next month’s meeting. If it comes later, the committee decides without it.

The Question row is fitted from the curriculum’s question for a different road, and says so here. It goes to the municipal town-planning office for a planner’s reply. What stays yours is how the school will count children walking before and after. What walking does for children’s weight is not the planner’s question either. Its owner is people who study physical activity in communities. Book 24, Physical activity and sedentary behaviour science, teaches that evidence.

blocks.prompt: A made-up line from a committee member: “Cycle lanes don’t work in India. I only need one document for that: the government’s own policy says nobody uses them. Spend the money on something else.” Name the signal that should have stopped the speaker, say what the policy actually says, and rewrite the line.
blocks.answer:
One source: the speaker rests the whole claim on one document and has misread it. The policy says “many”, not all, cycle tracks and pedestrian paths “do not get used as initially envisaged”. It reports “a view” that bad design is why. It proposes designing them in open debate with experts and users. It does not say they do not work in India. About to act follows: the committee may drop the lane on this line.

Rewrite: “The 2006 transport policy says many cycle tracks have gone unused, and reports a view that poor design is why. Whether this one would be used is outside what I can assess, and here is who can: the town-planning office. Let’s ask them before we decide.”
